#### ! Scenario

*Or what to do when you want to centralise versions*
This scenario demonstrates how to manage dependency versions centrally in sbt, the job Maven's `<dependencyManagement>` and Gradle's `platform()` do.

::: {.callout-note title="Tool Versions"}
This scenario was tested with **sbt 1.12**, which uses the **Coursier** resolver (the default since sbt 1.3). On sbt 1.x the older Ivy engine can still be selected with `useCoursier := false`; under Ivy, resolution edge cases differ and Ivy-only settings such as `conflictManager` apply (Coursier ignores them). `dependencyTree` is built in since **sbt 1.4**; earlier versions need the sbt-dependency-graph plugin. sbt 2.0 (June 2026) keeps these resolution rules, removes the Ivy opt-out, adds native BOM import, and turns Test-configuration eviction warnings into errors; the demos here target sbt 1.x.
sbt 1.x has no native BOM import. The technique shown here (a shared `val`) is the sbt 1.x idiom; sbt 2.0 can consume a Maven BOM directly.
:::

#### ! Example

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 4.4
graph LR
    Root[Project Root] --> LibA[lib-a:1.0.0]
    Root --> LibB[lib-b:1.0.0]
```

```{.scala include="build.sbt" snippet="s3-deps"}
```

#### ! Expect
Versions defined in one place (a `val`, or a `Dependencies` object under `project/`) are applied consistently across every module that uses them.

#### ! Why
An sbt build is a Scala program, so the ordinary tools of the language, values, objects and functions, serve as version management. A `val` is weaker than Maven's `<dependencyManagement>` in one respect: it only governs declarations that reference it. A transitive dependency that arrives with its own version is unaffected, and ordinary highest-wins resolution applies (SB2). To govern the whole graph you need `dependencyOverrides` (SB6).

#### ! Fix
*   **Variables:** define versions as `val`s at the top of `build.sbt`, or in `project/Dependencies.scala` for multi-module builds.
*   **BOM import:** sbt 1.x cannot import a Maven BOM natively. The [`here-sbt-bom`](https://github.com/heremaps/here-sbt-bom) plugin reads a BOM and feeds its versions into `dependencyOverrides`; sbt 2.0 adds native BOM support.
*   **Overrides:** pin versions graph-wide with `dependencyOverrides` when transitives must agree too (SB6, SB16).

#### ! Risk
* LOW One `val` per library family, referenced everywhere.
* MEDIUM Versions duplicated across modules because someone bypassed the shared object; drift follows.
* HIGH Assuming a central `val` controls transitive versions. It does not; only `dependencyOverrides` does.

#### ! Control
*   **`project/Dependencies.scala`:** for multi-module builds, define all dependencies and versions in a single Scala object. Modules reference `Dependencies.libA` rather than coordinates, so one edit moves the whole build.

#### ! Check

**Fast check:** `sbt dependencyTree`

**What to look for:** Every library versioned from the shared `val` shows that version, and no `(evicted by: …)` markers appear.

**Conclusion:** Central version definitions keep the direct declarations aligned.

#### ! Scales
As projects grow, `build.sbt` becomes crowded. Moving dependency definitions to `project/Dependencies.scala` is the standard Scala practice: group related dependencies ("testing", "database drivers") and manage their versions together. Organisations typically ship that object inside a shared sbt plugin so every repository inherits the same versions.

#### ! Takeaway
Use Scala values to centralise direct versions; use `dependencyOverrides` (or a BOM plugin, or sbt 2's native BOM import) when the whole graph must agree.

#### ! Wild

When Lightbend moved Akka from the Apache licence to the Business Source License in September 2022, thousands of Scala builds suddenly needed to hold every Akka module at `2.6.20`, the last Apache-licensed release, while teams decided between paying and migrating. Builds that already routed every Akka coordinate through one `val akkaVersion` changed a single line. Builds with versions scattered across modules spent days finding them all, and several discovered a transitive path had quietly pulled in a `2.7.x` artifact anyway, which only `dependencyOverrides` could stop.
